chapter_text:
CHAPTER 22 - DUAL NATURE OF RADIATION AND MATTER

Introduction

By the end of the nineteenth century the wave theory of light was firmly established. Interference, diffraction and polarisation had all been explained by treating light as an electromagnetic wave. Yet a group of experiments on the emission of electrons from metal surfaces refused to fit the wave picture. Their explanation, given by Albert Einstein in 1905, forced physicists to accept that light also behaves as a stream of particles (photons). A few years later Louis de Broglie turned the argument around and proposed that matter, too, has a wave nature. This chapter develops both ideas - the particle nature of radiation and the wave nature of matter - which together are called the DUAL NATURE of radiation and matter.

22.1 ELECTRON EMISSION AND WORK FUNCTION

A metal contains a large number of FREE ELECTRONS that move about randomly inside it. These electrons are held within the metal by the attraction of the positive ions of the lattice; they do not leave the surface on their own at ordinary temperatures. To pull a free electron out of the metal, a certain minimum amount of energy must be supplied to it. This minimum energy required to just free an electron from the surface of a metal is called the WORK FUNCTION of the metal, denoted phi0 (phi-nought). Work function is usually measured in electron volt (eV), where 1 eV = 1.6 x 10^-19 joule. Different metals have different work functions - for example caesium has a low work function (about 2.14 eV) while platinum has a high one (about 5.6 eV).

The energy needed for emission can be supplied in several ways, giving four types of electron emission:
 (a) THERMIONIC EMISSION - the metal is heated, so that thermal energy raises some electrons above the work function and they escape. This is used in the cathode of vacuum tubes.
 (b) FIELD (or COLD-CATHODE) EMISSION - a very strong electric field (of the order of 10^8 V/m) applied at the surface pulls electrons out.
 (c) PHOTOELECTRIC EMISSION - light of suitable frequency falling on the metal supplies energy to the electrons, which are then emitted. This is the subject of most of this chapter.
 (d) SECONDARY EMISSION - fast-moving electrons or ions strike the surface and knock out other electrons.

22.2 THE PHOTOELECTRIC EFFECT - EARLY OBSERVATIONS

In 1887 Heinrich Hertz, while producing electromagnetic waves with a spark gap, noticed that a spark passed more easily when ultraviolet light fell on the negative electrode. Wilhelm Hallwachs and Philipp Lenard studied the effect in detail between 1886 and 1902. They found that when light of high enough frequency falls on a metal surface, electrons are emitted from it. These emitted electrons are called PHOTOELECTRONS and the phenomenon is the PHOTOELECTRIC EFFECT. Lenard showed that the particles emitted were indeed electrons, identical to those found in cathode rays.

22.3 EXPERIMENTAL STUDY OF THE PHOTOELECTRIC EFFECT

The effect is studied using an evacuated glass tube containing two electrodes - an emitting plate (the emitter or cathode C) and a collecting plate (the collector or anode A). Monochromatic light of known frequency and intensity is allowed to fall on the emitter through a quartz window (quartz transmits ultraviolet). A variable potential difference is applied between the plates, and the photoelectric current is measured with a sensitive microammeter. By varying the intensity, the frequency and the collector potential, three sets of observations are obtained.

Effect of INTENSITY of light: When the frequency and the collector potential are kept fixed, the photoelectric current is found to be directly proportional to the intensity of the incident light. Greater intensity means more photoelectrons are emitted per second, so the current (which measures the number of electrons collected per second) is larger. Intensity does NOT change the energy of the individual photoelectrons.

Effect of POTENTIAL: For a fixed frequency and intensity, as the positive potential of the collector is increased, the current rises and eventually reaches a constant maximum value called the SATURATION CURRENT - at this stage every emitted electron reaches the collector. If instead the collector is made negative with respect to the emitter (a retarding potential), the current falls. At a particular negative voltage the current becomes zero - even the most energetic electrons are turned back. This minimum retarding voltage that just stops the fastest photoelectrons is called the STOPPING POTENTIAL, V0. At the stopping potential the work done against the field equals the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons:
   e V0 = K_max = (1/2) m v_max^2

Effect of FREQUENCY: A crucial result is obtained by changing the frequency of the light. For each metal there is a certain minimum frequency, called the THRESHOLD FREQUENCY f0, below which NO photoelectrons are emitted, no matter how intense the light or how long it shines. Above f0, the stopping potential (and hence the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons) increases linearly with frequency but is INDEPENDENT of intensity. When V0 is plotted against frequency f, a straight line is obtained whose slope is the same (h/e) for all metals; the line meets the frequency axis at f0.

22.4 LAWS OF PHOTOELECTRIC EMISSION

The experimental results are summarised in four laws:
 1. For a given metal and frequency, the number of photoelectrons emitted per second (the photoelectric current) is directly proportional to the intensity of the incident light.
 2. For every metal there is a threshold frequency f0. Light of frequency below f0 cannot cause emission, whatever its intensity.
 3. Above the threshold frequency, the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons increases with the frequency of the light and does not depend on its intensity.
 4. Photoelectric emission is an INSTANTANEOUS process - there is no measurable time lag (less than about 10^-9 s) between the arrival of light and the emission of electrons, even for very feeble light.

22.5 FAILURE OF THE WAVE THEORY

The classical wave theory of light could not explain these laws. According to the wave picture, the energy of a wave is spread uniformly over the wavefront and depends on the intensity, not on the frequency. Therefore:
 (i) A wave of any frequency should, if intense enough, deliver sufficient energy to eject electrons - so there should be NO threshold frequency. Experiment contradicts this.
 (ii) The maximum kinetic energy of the electrons should increase with intensity (brighter light), not with frequency. Experiment shows the opposite.
 (iii) For feeble light, an electron would need to accumulate energy over a long time before escaping, so emission should show a time lag. In fact emission is instantaneous.
These three disagreements showed that the wave theory, successful for interference and diffraction, fails completely for the photoelectric effect.

22.6 EINSTEIN'S PHOTOELECTRIC EQUATION

In 1905 Einstein explained the effect by extending Planck's quantum idea. He proposed that light of frequency f consists of discrete packets of energy called QUANTA or PHOTONS, each carrying energy
   E = h f
where h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s is Planck's constant. In the photoelectric effect a single photon is absorbed by a single electron, giving up all its energy at once. Part of this energy (phi0) is used to free the electron from the metal; the rest appears as the kinetic energy of the electron. For an electron ejected from the surface with the maximum possible kinetic energy,
   K_max = h f - phi0
This is EINSTEIN'S PHOTOELECTRIC EQUATION. Since phi0 = h f0 (the work function equals the energy of a threshold-frequency photon), the equation can also be written
   K_max = h f - h f0 = h (f - f0)
and, in terms of stopping potential,
   e V0 = h f - phi0.

This single equation explains every observed law:
 - If f is less than f0, then h f is less than phi0 and K_max would be negative - impossible - so no emission occurs. This gives the threshold frequency.
 - K_max depends only on f (through h f) and on phi0, not on intensity. This explains why the maximum kinetic energy rises with frequency and is independent of intensity.
 - Greater intensity means more photons per second, hence more photoelectrons per second and a larger current, but the same K_max per electron.
 - Because one photon is absorbed by one electron in a single event, emission is instantaneous.
The graph of V0 against f is a straight line of slope h/e, and multiplying the slope by e gives a direct measurement of Planck's constant h - as Millikan confirmed in 1916.

22.7 THE PHOTON PICTURE OF LIGHT

A photon is a quantum of electromagnetic radiation with the following properties. It has energy E = h f = h c / lambda, where c is the speed of light and lambda the wavelength. Although a photon has no rest mass, it carries momentum
   p = E / c = h f / c = h / lambda.
Photons travel at the speed of light, are electrically neutral, and are not deflected by electric or magnetic fields. In any interaction with matter, energy and momentum are conserved. The number of photons in a beam is proportional to its intensity. Thus light shows a PARTICLE nature in emission and absorption (photoelectric effect, Compton effect) while still showing a WAVE nature in propagation (interference, diffraction). This is the dual nature of radiation.

22.8 DE BROGLIE HYPOTHESIS - MATTER WAVES

In 1924 Louis de Broglie made a bold proposal: if radiation, long regarded as a wave, can behave like particles, then material particles such as electrons should also behave like waves. He suggested that a particle of momentum p = m v has associated with it a wavelength
   lambda = h / p = h / (m v).
This is the DE BROGLIE WAVELENGTH and the associated wave is called a MATTER WAVE. The relation is the same as for a photon (lambda = h / p), which shows the pleasing symmetry between radiation and matter. Because h is extremely small, the wavelength of an ordinary object (say a cricket ball) is far too small to detect; only for very light particles like electrons does the wave nature become observable.

For an electron accelerated from rest through a potential difference of V volt, the kinetic energy gained is e V = (1/2) m v^2, so the momentum is p = sqrt(2 m e V). Substituting the values of h, m and e gives a convenient formula for the de Broglie wavelength of the electron:
   lambda = 12.27 / sqrt(V)  angstrom   (with V in volt, 1 angstrom = 10^-10 m).
For example, an electron accelerated through 100 V has lambda = 12.27 / sqrt(100) = 1.227 angstrom - comparable to the spacing of atoms in a crystal, and hence capable of being diffracted by a crystal.

22.9 DAVISSON-GERMER EXPERIMENT

The wave nature of the electron was confirmed experimentally in 1927 by C. J. Davisson and L. H. Germer in the United States (and independently by G. P. Thomson). In their apparatus, electrons from a heated filament were accelerated through a known potential difference and directed as a fine beam onto a single crystal of nickel. The electrons scattered by the regular array of atoms were collected by a movable detector that measured the intensity of the scattered beam at different angles.

They found that the scattered intensity showed a distinct PEAK at a particular angle for a particular accelerating voltage. For 54 V, a strong peak appeared at a scattering angle of 50 degrees. Such a peak is exactly what one expects if the electron beam is being DIFFRACTED by the regularly spaced atoms of the crystal, just as X-rays are diffracted. From the crystal geometry the wavelength of the electrons was calculated to be about 1.65 angstrom. The de Broglie formula predicts lambda = 12.27 / sqrt(54) = 1.67 angstrom for 54 V electrons - in excellent agreement. The experiment thus provided direct proof that electrons behave as waves with exactly the wavelength predicted by de Broglie, establishing the wave nature of matter.

SUMMARY

- The work function phi0 is the minimum energy needed to free an electron from a metal surface. Electrons can be emitted by thermionic, field, photoelectric and secondary emission.
- In the photoelectric effect, light of frequency above a threshold f0 ejects electrons from a metal. The photoelectric current is proportional to intensity; the stopping potential (and K_max) depends on frequency, not intensity; emission is instantaneous.
- The wave theory fails to explain the threshold frequency, the intensity-independence of K_max, and the absence of a time lag.
- Einstein treated light as photons of energy E = h f and obtained K_max = h f - phi0 = h (f - f0), with e V0 = h f - phi0. This explains all the laws and lets h be measured.
- A photon has energy E = h f = h c / lambda and momentum p = h / lambda, showing the particle nature of radiation.
- De Broglie proposed matter waves of wavelength lambda = h / p = h / (m v). For an electron accelerated through V volt, lambda = 12.27 / sqrt(V) angstrom.
- The Davisson-Germer experiment (electron diffraction by a nickel crystal) confirmed the wave nature of matter, with the measured wavelength matching de Broglie's prediction.

topics.description: The photon as a quantum of radiation; energy E = h f = h c / lambda; momentum p = E/c = h/lambda; photons neutral, massless (rest mass zero) and travelling at the speed of light; the dual (wave-particle) nature of radiation.

chapter_summary.title: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This is the NIOS Senior Secondary Physics (312) summary for the chapter on the dual nature of radiation and matter. It covers electron emission and the work function, the photoelectric effect and its laws, the failure of the wave theory, Einstein's photoelectric equation, the photon picture of light, the de Broglie hypothesis of matter waves, and the Davisson-Germer experiment that confirmed it.

sections.heading: Electron emission and work function
bullets: A metal holds its free electrons by the attraction of the lattice ions; the minimum energy needed to free an electron from the surface is the work function phi0, measured in electron-volt (1 eV = 1.6 x 10^-19 J).
Energy can be supplied by heat (thermionic emission), by a strong electric field (field emission), by light (photoelectric emission), or by bombardment with fast particles (secondary emission).
The work function is related to the threshold frequency by phi0 = h f0.

sections.heading: The photoelectric effect and its experimental study
bullets: Hertz (1887), Hallwachs and Lenard found that light of high enough frequency ejects electrons (photoelectrons) from a metal surface.
The photoelectric current is directly proportional to the intensity of the light and rises to a saturation value as the collector potential is increased.
The stopping potential V0 is the retarding voltage that just stops the fastest photoelectrons: e V0 = K_max. It depends on frequency, not on intensity.
Below the threshold frequency f0, no electrons are emitted however intense the light; emission above f0 is instantaneous.

sections.heading: Laws of photoelectric emission and failure of the wave theory
bullets: Laws: current is proportional to intensity; there is a threshold frequency; K_max increases with frequency and is independent of intensity; emission is instantaneous.
The wave theory predicts no threshold frequency, K_max increasing with intensity, and a time lag for feeble light - all contradicted by experiment.
Hence the classical wave theory, though successful for interference and diffraction, fails to explain the photoelectric effect.

sections.heading: Einstein's photoelectric equation and the photon
bullets: Einstein treated light as photons of energy E = h f; one photon is absorbed by one electron.
The energy balance gives K_max = h f - phi0 = h(f - f0), and e V0 = h f - phi0.
This explains the threshold frequency, the frequency-dependence of K_max, its independence of intensity, and the instantaneous emission.
A photon has energy E = h f = h c/lambda and momentum p = h/lambda; it is massless (zero rest mass) and neutral, showing the particle nature of radiation.

sections.heading: Matter waves and the Davisson-Germer experiment
bullets: de Broglie proposed that a particle of momentum p = m v has a wavelength lambda = h/p = h/(m v).
For an electron accelerated through V volt, lambda = 12.27/sqrt(V) angstrom; e.g. 100 V gives 1.227 angstrom.
Davisson and Germer directed electrons at a nickel crystal and observed a diffraction peak (54 V, 50 degrees) corresponding to lambda about 1.65 angstrom.
This matched the de Broglie prediction (1.67 angstrom), confirming the wave nature of matter.

key_takeaways: The work function phi0 is the minimum energy needed to free an electron from a metal; electrons are emitted thermionically, by field, photoelectrically or by secondary emission.
The photoelectric current is proportional to intensity, but the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons depends only on the frequency of the light (above a threshold frequency f0).
The classical wave theory fails: it cannot explain the threshold frequency, the frequency-dependence of K_max, or the absence of a time lag.
Einstein's equation K_max = h f - phi0 = h(f - f0), with e V0 = h f - phi0, explains all the observations and gives h from the slope of the V0 versus f graph.
A photon carries energy E = h f = h c/lambda and momentum p = h/lambda - light has a particle nature.
de Broglie's matter waves have wavelength lambda = h/(m v); for an electron lambda = 12.27/sqrt(V) angstrom.
The Davisson-Germer experiment confirmed the wave nature of matter through electron diffraction by a nickel crystal.

glossary.definition: The minimum energy required to free an electron from the surface of a metal, usually measured in electron-volt.
The energy gained by an electron moving through a potential difference of 1 volt; 1 eV = 1.6 x 10^-19 joule.
Emission of electrons from a metal when it is heated so that thermal energy exceeds the work function.
Emission of electrons from a metal surface under a very strong external electric field.
The emission of electrons from a metal surface when light of frequency above the threshold frequency falls on it.
An electron emitted from a metal surface in the photoelectric effect.
The minimum frequency of incident light that can cause photoelectric emission from a given metal; below it no electrons are emitted.
The retarding voltage that just stops the most energetic photoelectrons, so that e V0 = K_max.
The maximum photoelectric current, reached when every emitted photoelectron is collected.
A quantum (packet) of electromagnetic radiation of energy E = h f and momentum p = h/lambda; massless and neutral, travelling at the speed of light.
A fundamental constant, h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s, relating a photon's energy to its frequency by E = h f.
K_max = h f - phi0 = h(f - f0), giving the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons in terms of frequency and work function.
The wavelength lambda = h/p = h/(m v) associated with a moving particle of momentum p.
The wave associated with a moving material particle, as proposed by de Broglie.
An experiment in which electrons diffracted by a nickel crystal showed a wavelength matching the de Broglie prediction, confirming the wave nature of matter.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Take Planck's constant h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s, charge of electron e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, speed of light c = 3 x 10^8 m/s, and mass of electron m = 9.11 x 10^-31 kg where required. Useful relation: photon energy in eV = 1240 / (wavelength in nm).

questions.question: Define the work function of a metal. In what unit is it usually expressed, and how is it related to the threshold frequency?
questions.answer: The WORK FUNCTION phi0 of a metal is the minimum energy required to just free an electron from the surface of the metal. It is usually expressed in electron-volt (eV), where 1 eV = 1.6 x 10^-19 J. It is related to the threshold frequency f0 by phi0 = h f0, where h is Planck's constant - that is, the work function equals the energy of a photon whose frequency is the threshold frequency.
questions.explanation: Definition + unit + relation phi0 = h f0.

questions.question: State the four laws of photoelectric emission.
questions.answer:
1. For a given metal and frequency, the number of photoelectrons emitted per second (the photoelectric current) is directly proportional to the intensity of the incident light.
2. For every metal there is a threshold frequency f0; light below f0 causes no emission, whatever its intensity.
3. Above f0, the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons increases with the frequency of the light and is independent of intensity.
4. Photoelectric emission is instantaneous - there is no measurable time lag between illumination and emission.
questions.explanation: The four experimental laws.

questions.question: Explain why the classical wave theory of light cannot account for the existence of a threshold frequency.
questions.answer: According to the wave theory, the energy of a light wave depends on its intensity (amplitude), not its frequency, and is spread continuously over the wavefront. Hence a wave of ANY frequency, if made intense enough, should deliver enough energy to eject electrons. This predicts that there should be NO threshold frequency - emission should be possible at any frequency provided the light is bright enough. Experiment shows the opposite: below f0 no emission occurs however intense the light. So the wave theory fails.
questions.explanation: Wave energy depends on intensity, not frequency, so no threshold is predicted.

questions.question: Light of wavelength 400 nm falls on a metal of work function 2.0 eV. Calculate (a) the energy of each photon in eV, (b) the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons, and (c) the stopping potential.
questions.answer:
(a) Photon energy E = 1240 / lambda(nm) = 1240 / 400 = 3.1 eV.
(b) By Einstein's equation, K_max = E - phi0 = 3.1 - 2.0 = 1.1 eV = 1.1 x 1.6 x 10^-19 = 1.76 x 10^-19 J.
(c) e V0 = K_max, so V0 = K_max / e = 1.1 eV / e = 1.1 V.
questions.explanation: Use E = 1240/lambda(nm); K_max = E - phi0; V0 = K_max(eV)/1.

questions.question: The work function of sodium is 2.28 eV. Find its threshold wavelength.
questions.answer: At threshold, phi0 = h c / lambda0, so lambda0 = 1240 / phi0(eV) nm = 1240 / 2.28 = 544 nm (about 5440 angstrom). Light of wavelength longer than 544 nm (lower frequency) cannot eject electrons from sodium.
questions.explanation: lambda0 = 1240/phi0(eV) nm.

questions.question: Calculate the energy (in joule and in eV) and the momentum of a photon of wavelength 500 nm.
questions.explanation: E = hc/lambda, p = h/lambda.

questions.question: State the de Broglie hypothesis and calculate the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through a potential difference of 100 V.
questions.answer: de Broglie hypothesis: a moving particle of momentum p = m v has an associated wave of wavelength lambda = h/p = h/(m v). For an electron accelerated through V volt, lambda = 12.27/sqrt(V) angstrom. For V = 100 V: lambda = 12.27/sqrt(100) = 12.27/10 = 1.227 angstrom = 1.227 x 10^-10 m.
questions.explanation: lambda = h/(mv); electron formula lambda = 12.27/sqrt(V) angstrom.

questions.question: Describe the Davisson-Germer experiment and explain how it confirms the wave nature of matter.
questions.answer:
Apparatus: electrons from a heated filament are accelerated through a known potential difference and formed into a fine beam directed at a single crystal of nickel. A movable detector measures the intensity of electrons scattered at different angles.

Observation: the scattered intensity shows a sharp PEAK at a definite angle for a definite accelerating voltage. For 54 V electrons a strong peak appears at a scattering angle of 50 degrees. Such a maximum is characteristic of DIFFRACTION - the regularly spaced atoms of the crystal act like a grating, exactly as they do for X-rays.

Analysis: from the crystal spacing and the angle, the wavelength of the electrons is found to be about 1.65 angstrom. The de Broglie formula predicts lambda = 12.27/sqrt(54) = 1.67 angstrom for 54 V electrons. The measured and predicted values agree closely.

Conclusion: electrons are diffracted like waves and their wavelength is exactly what de Broglie predicted. This is direct experimental proof of the wave nature of matter.
questions.explanation: Setup, diffraction peak, wavelength comparison, conclusion.

questions.question: In an experiment the stopping potential for a metal is 1.5 V when light of frequency 8.0 x 10^14 Hz is used. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons and the work function of the metal.
questions.explanation: K_max = eV0; phi0 = hf - K_max.

questions.question: Name the four types of electron emission and state briefly how each is produced.
questions.answer:
1. Thermionic emission - electrons are emitted when the metal is heated, thermal energy lifting them above the work function.
2. Field (cold-cathode) emission - a very strong external electric field pulls electrons out of the surface.
3. Photoelectric emission - light of suitable (high enough) frequency supplies energy to free the electrons.
4. Secondary emission - fast-moving electrons or ions strike the surface and knock out other electrons.
questions.explanation: The four emission mechanisms and their energy sources.

questions.question: What is meant by the work function of a metal?
questions.answer: The work function phi0 of a metal is the minimum amount of energy that must be supplied to a free electron at the surface of the metal to just free it from the metal. It is usually measured in electron-volt. Different metals have different work functions.
questions.explanation: Definition and unit.

questions.question: Name and briefly explain the four types of electron emission.
questions.answer:
1. Thermionic emission - heating the metal gives electrons enough thermal energy to escape.
2. Field emission - a very strong electric field at the surface pulls electrons out.
3. Photoelectric emission - light of suitable frequency supplies energy to free the electrons.
4. Secondary emission - fast electrons or ions strike the surface and knock out other electrons.
questions.explanation: Four mechanisms with energy sources.

questions.question: Define the electron-volt and relate the work function to the threshold frequency.
questions.answer: One electron-volt (eV) is the energy gained by an electron when it moves through a potential difference of one volt: 1 eV = 1.6 x 10^-19 J. The work function is related to the threshold frequency by phi0 = h f0, so a photon of the threshold frequency has energy just equal to the work function.
questions.explanation: eV definition and phi0 = h f0.

questions.question: The work function of a metal is 3.3 x 10^-19 J. Find its threshold frequency and threshold wavelength.
questions.answer:
Threshold frequency f0 = phi0/h = 3.3 x 10^-19 / 6.63 x 10^-34 = 4.98 x 10^14 Hz (about 5.0 x 10^14 Hz).
Threshold wavelength lambda0 = c/f0 = 3 x 10^8 / 4.98 x 10^14 = 6.02 x 10^-7 m = 602 nm.
questions.explanation: f0 = phi0/h; lambda0 = c/f0.

questions.question: What is the stopping potential? Write its relation to the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons.
questions.answer: The stopping potential V0 is the minimum retarding (negative) collector voltage at which the photoelectric current becomes zero, i.e. the voltage that just stops the most energetic photoelectrons. It is related to the maximum kinetic energy by e V0 = K_max.
questions.explanation: Definition and e V0 = K_max.

questions.question: Describe how the photoelectric current varies (a) with intensity and (b) with collector potential.
questions.answer:
(a) For fixed frequency and potential, the photoelectric current is directly proportional to the intensity of the light - more intense light emits more photoelectrons per second.
(b) As the positive collector potential is increased, the current rises and then becomes constant at the saturation value (all electrons collected). If the collector is made negative, the current falls and becomes zero at the stopping potential.
questions.explanation: Intensity: proportional; potential: rises to saturation, zero at V0.

questions.question: What is the threshold frequency? What happens if the incident frequency is below it?
questions.answer: The threshold frequency f0 is the minimum frequency of incident light needed to cause photoelectric emission from a given metal. If the incident frequency is below f0, no photoelectrons are emitted at all, no matter how intense the light or how long it shines.
questions.explanation: Definition; no emission below f0.

questions.question: Explain how the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons and the photoelectric current depend on intensity and frequency.
questions.answer: Photoelectric current (number of electrons per second) depends only on INTENSITY - it is proportional to intensity and independent of frequency (above f0). Maximum kinetic energy K_max depends only on FREQUENCY - it increases linearly with frequency and is completely independent of intensity. Thus brighter light gives more electrons but not more energetic ones; higher-frequency light gives more energetic electrons but not more of them.
questions.explanation: Current: intensity; K_max: frequency.

questions.question: State the four laws of photoelectric emission.
questions.answer:
1. The photoelectric current is directly proportional to the intensity of the incident light (for fixed frequency).
2. For each metal there is a threshold frequency f0 below which no emission occurs.
3. The maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons increases with frequency and is independent of intensity.
4. Photoelectric emission is instantaneous (no time lag).
questions.explanation: The four laws.

questions.question: Give two reasons why the wave theory of light fails to explain the photoelectric effect.
questions.answer:
1. The wave theory says the energy of light depends on its intensity, not frequency, so it predicts no threshold frequency and predicts K_max should increase with intensity - both contrary to experiment.
2. For feeble light the wave theory predicts a time lag, because an electron would need time to accumulate enough energy from the spread-out wave; but experiment shows emission is instantaneous.
questions.explanation: No threshold predicted; predicts time lag.

questions.question: On the wave picture, why would there be a time delay for emission with feeble light, and what is actually observed?
questions.answer: On the wave picture, the energy of the light is spread continuously over the whole wavefront, so a single electron receives only a tiny fraction of it. With feeble light it would take a long time for an electron to accumulate energy equal to the work function, predicting a measurable time delay. In fact, experiments show that emission begins essentially instantaneously (within about 10^-9 s), even for very weak light - which the photon picture explains through single-photon absorption.
questions.explanation: Predicted lag vs observed instantaneous emission.

questions.question: Write Einstein's photoelectric equation and explain each term.
questions.answer: K_max = h f - phi0, where K_max is the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons, h f is the energy of the incident photon (h = Planck's constant, f = frequency), and phi0 is the work function of the metal. It can also be written K_max = h(f - f0) and e V0 = h f - phi0.
questions.explanation: Meaning of each symbol.

questions.question: Show how Einstein's equation explains the existence of a threshold frequency and the independence of K_max from intensity.
questions.answer: From K_max = h f - phi0: for emission K_max must be positive, so h f must exceed phi0, i.e. f > phi0/h = f0. Below f0, h f < phi0 and emission is impossible - this is the threshold frequency. K_max depends only on f and phi0, not on how many photons arrive, so it is independent of intensity. Greater intensity means more photons and hence more photoelectrons per second (larger current) but the same K_max per electron.
questions.explanation: Threshold from hf>phi0; K_max independent of intensity.

questions.question: Light of wavelength 300 nm is incident on a metal of work function 2.0 eV. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons and the stopping potential.
questions.answer:
Photon energy E = 1240/300 = 4.13 eV.
K_max = E - phi0 = 4.13 - 2.0 = 2.13 eV = 2.13 x 1.6 x 10^-19 = 3.41 x 10^-19 J.
Stopping potential V0 = K_max/e = 2.13 V.
questions.explanation: E=1240/lambda(nm); K_max=E-phi0; V0=K_max(eV).

questions.question: When light of frequency 1.0 x 10^15 Hz falls on a metal, the stopping potential is 2.0 V. Find the work function of the metal in eV.
questions.answer:
Photon energy E = h f = 6.63 x 10^-34 x 1.0 x 10^15 = 6.63 x 10^-19 J = 4.14 eV.
K_max = e V0 = 2.0 eV.
Work function phi0 = E - K_max = 4.14 - 2.0 = 2.14 eV (about 3.43 x 10^-19 J). This is close to the work function of caesium.
questions.explanation: phi0 = hf - eV0.

questions.question: The threshold wavelength of a metal is 600 nm. Will light of wavelength 400 nm cause photoelectric emission? Explain.
questions.answer: Threshold wavelength lambda0 = 600 nm corresponds to threshold frequency f0. Light of 400 nm has a SHORTER wavelength and hence HIGHER frequency than the threshold. Since its frequency exceeds f0 (photon energy 1240/400 = 3.1 eV is greater than the work function 1240/600 = 2.07 eV), it WILL cause emission, with K_max = 3.1 - 2.07 = 1.03 eV.
questions.explanation: Shorter wavelength -> higher frequency > f0 -> emission occurs.

questions.question: List four properties of a photon.
questions.answer:
1. A photon has energy E = h f = h c/lambda.
2. It carries momentum p = h/lambda even though it has zero rest mass.
3. It is electrically neutral, so it is not deflected by electric or magnetic fields.
4. It travels at the speed of light in vacuum, and the number of photons in a beam is proportional to the beam's intensity.
questions.explanation: Energy, momentum, neutral/massless, speed c.

questions.question: Calculate the energy and momentum of a photon of wavelength 620 nm.
questions.explanation: E=hc/lambda; p=h/lambda.

questions.question: Explain what is meant by the dual nature of radiation.
questions.answer: The dual nature of radiation means that light behaves both as a wave and as a stream of particles. In propagation phenomena such as interference, diffraction and polarisation, light shows its WAVE nature. In its interaction with matter - emission and absorption, as in the photoelectric effect and the Compton effect - light behaves as a stream of PARTICLES (photons) of energy h f and momentum h/lambda. Both aspects are needed for a complete description.
questions.explanation: Wave in propagation, particle in interaction.

questions.question: State the de Broglie hypothesis and write the expression for the de Broglie wavelength.
questions.answer: de Broglie proposed that every moving material particle has an associated wave (a matter wave). A particle of momentum p = m v has a de Broglie wavelength lambda = h/p = h/(m v), where h is Planck's constant. The same relation lambda = h/p also holds for a photon.
questions.explanation: Hypothesis + lambda = h/(m v).

questions.question: Derive the formula lambda = 12.27/sqrt(V) angstrom for an electron accelerated through V volt.
questions.answer: An electron accelerated from rest through potential difference V gains kinetic energy e V = (1/2) m v^2, so its momentum is p = m v = sqrt(2 m e V). Its de Broglie wavelength is lambda = h/p = h/sqrt(2 m e V). Substituting h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s, m = 9.11 x 10^-31 kg and e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C gives lambda = 12.27/sqrt(V) x 10^-10 m = 12.27/sqrt(V) angstrom, with V in volt.
questions.explanation: p = sqrt(2meV); substitute constants.

questions.question: Find the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through 200 V.
questions.explanation: Substitute V=200 in the electron formula.

questions.question: Explain the meaning of work function and describe the four types of electron emission with one use of each.
questions.answer:
A metal contains many free electrons that move about inside it but are held in by the attraction of the positive lattice ions. The WORK FUNCTION phi0 is the minimum energy that must be given to a surface electron to just set it free; it is measured in electron-volt and differs from metal to metal.

Four ways of supplying this energy give four types of emission:
1. THERMIONIC EMISSION - the metal is heated; thermal energy raises some electrons above the work function so they escape. Used in the heated cathodes of vacuum tubes and older TV picture tubes.
2. FIELD (COLD-CATHODE) EMISSION - a very strong electric field (about 10^8 V/m) at the surface pulls electrons out. Used in field-emission microscopes and some electron sources.
3. PHOTOELECTRIC EMISSION - light of frequency above the threshold supplies the energy. Used in photocells and light meters.
4. SECONDARY EMISSION - fast electrons or ions strike the surface and knock out further electrons. Used in photomultiplier tubes.
questions.explanation: Work function + four emission types with uses.

questions.question: With the help of the experimental arrangement, describe the effect of intensity, potential and frequency on the photoelectric current.
questions.answer:
Apparatus: an evacuated tube contains an emitting plate (cathode C) and a collecting plate (anode A). Monochromatic light of known frequency and intensity enters through a quartz window and falls on C. A variable potential is applied between the plates and the current measured by a microammeter.

Effect of intensity: with frequency and potential fixed, the photoelectric current is directly proportional to the intensity of light - more intense light ejects more photoelectrons per second. The energy of each electron is unchanged.

Effect of potential: with frequency and intensity fixed, increasing the positive collector potential raises the current until it becomes constant at the SATURATION value (every emitted electron is collected). Making the collector negative reduces the current; at the STOPPING POTENTIAL V0 the current is zero, since even the fastest electrons are turned back, and e V0 = K_max.

Effect of frequency: below the THRESHOLD FREQUENCY f0 no electrons are emitted, whatever the intensity. Above f0, the stopping potential (and K_max) increases linearly with frequency but does not depend on intensity. A graph of V0 against f is a straight line of slope h/e.
questions.explanation: Apparatus + intensity, potential, frequency effects.

questions.question: State the laws of photoelectric emission and explain in detail why the classical wave theory fails to account for them.
questions.answer:
Laws of photoelectric emission:
1. Photoelectric current is directly proportional to the intensity of the incident light (fixed frequency).
2. For each metal there is a threshold frequency f0 below which no emission occurs, whatever the intensity.
3. The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons increases with the frequency of light and is independent of intensity.
4. Emission is instantaneous - there is no measurable time lag.

Failure of the wave theory:
(i) In the wave picture the energy of light depends on its intensity (amplitude), not on frequency, and is spread over the wavefront. So a wave of any frequency, if intense enough, should eject electrons - predicting NO threshold frequency. This contradicts Law 2.
(ii) The wave picture predicts that the kinetic energy of the electrons should increase with intensity (a brighter wave carries more energy), whereas experiment shows K_max depends on frequency and not on intensity. This contradicts Law 3.
(iii) For feeble light, an electron would need a long time to accumulate enough energy from the spread-out wave, so emission should be delayed. In fact it is instantaneous. This contradicts Law 4.

These failures were resolved only by Einstein's photon theory.
questions.explanation: Four laws + three-fold failure of wave theory.

questions.question: State Einstein's photoelectric equation. Using it, explain all the observed laws of photoelectric emission, and describe how it allows Planck's constant to be measured.
questions.answer:
Einstein assumed light of frequency f consists of photons of energy E = h f. In the photoelectric effect a single photon is absorbed by a single electron; part of the energy (phi0) frees the electron and the rest becomes its kinetic energy. For the fastest electrons:
   K_max = h f - phi0 = h(f - f0),   and   e V0 = h f - phi0.

Explanation of the laws:
- Threshold frequency: emission needs K_max > 0, so h f > phi0, i.e. f > f0 = phi0/h. Below f0 there is no emission (Law 2).
- K_max versus frequency: K_max = h f - phi0 increases linearly with f and does not involve intensity (Law 3).
- Current versus intensity: greater intensity means more photons per second, hence more photoelectrons per second and a larger current, but the same K_max (Law 1).
- Instantaneous emission: because one photon is absorbed by one electron in a single event, emission has no time lag (Law 4).

Measuring h: writing e V0 = h f - phi0 gives V0 = (h/e) f - phi0/e. A graph of stopping potential V0 against frequency f is a straight line of slope h/e. Measuring this slope and multiplying by e gives Planck's constant h. Millikan carried out exactly this measurement in 1916, confirming Einstein's theory.
questions.explanation: Equation + explanation of all laws + slope method for h.

questions.question: Describe the photon picture of light and hence explain the dual nature of radiation.
questions.explanation: Photon properties + wave/particle duality.

questions.question: State the de Broglie hypothesis. Obtain the expression for the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through a potential difference V, and calculate it for V = 54 V.
questions.answer:
de Broglie hypothesis: any moving material particle has an associated matter wave of wavelength lambda = h/p = h/(m v), where p = m v is the momentum. This mirrors the photon relation lambda = h/p, giving a symmetry between radiation and matter.

Electron accelerated through V: the kinetic energy gained is e V = (1/2) m v^2, so p = m v = sqrt(2 m e V). Hence
   lambda = h/sqrt(2 m e V).
Putting h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s, m = 9.11 x 10^-31 kg, e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C gives the convenient form
   lambda = 12.27/sqrt(V) angstrom (V in volt).

For V = 54 V: lambda = 12.27/sqrt(54) = 12.27/7.35 = 1.67 angstrom = 1.67 x 10^-10 m. This is the value that matched the Davisson-Germer result.
questions.explanation: Hypothesis, derivation, and 54 V value.

questions.question: Explain the meaning of the electron-volt and the relation phi0 = h f0. The work function of caesium is 2.14 eV; find its threshold frequency and threshold wavelength.
questions.answer:
One electron-volt (eV) is the energy gained by an electron when it is accelerated through a potential difference of one volt: 1 eV = 1.6 x 10^-19 J. Work functions and photon energies are conveniently expressed in this unit.

The work function phi0 is the energy of a photon whose frequency is exactly the threshold frequency f0, so phi0 = h f0. Equivalently f0 = phi0/h and the threshold wavelength is lambda0 = c/f0 = h c/phi0.

For caesium, phi0 = 2.14 eV = 2.14 x 1.6 x 10^-19 = 3.42 x 10^-19 J.
Threshold frequency f0 = phi0/h = 3.42 x 10^-19 / 6.63 x 10^-34 = 5.17 x 10^14 Hz.
Threshold wavelength lambda0 = c/f0 = 3 x 10^8 / 5.17 x 10^14 = 5.80 x 10^-7 m = 580 nm (about 5800 angstrom). Light of wavelength shorter than 580 nm can eject electrons from caesium.
questions.explanation: eV definition, phi0=h f0, and caesium f0 and lambda0.

questions.question: Describe the Davisson-Germer experiment in detail and explain how it confirms the wave nature of matter. Include the comparison of measured and predicted wavelengths.
questions.answer:
Aim: to test de Broglie's hypothesis that electrons behave as waves.

Apparatus and method: electrons emitted by a heated filament are accelerated through a known, adjustable potential difference and formed into a narrow beam. The beam strikes a single crystal of nickel. Electrons scattered by the regularly arranged atoms of the crystal are received by a detector (a Faraday collector) that can be moved to measure the scattered intensity at different angles.

Observations: for a fixed accelerating voltage the scattered intensity is not uniform; it shows a sharp PEAK at a definite scattering angle. When the electrons are accelerated through 54 V, a strong peak appears at a scattering angle of 50 degrees. A maximum of this kind is exactly what happens when waves are DIFFRACTED by a regular array of scatterers - the crystal acts like a diffraction grating, just as it does for X-rays.

Analysis: from the known spacing of the nickel atoms and the angle of the peak, the wavelength of the electrons is calculated to be about 1.65 angstrom. The de Broglie formula predicts lambda = 12.27/sqrt(54) = 1.67 angstrom for 54 V electrons. The measured and predicted values agree very closely.

Conclusion: the electron beam is diffracted like a wave, and its wavelength is exactly what de Broglie predicted. The experiment is therefore direct experimental proof of the wave nature of matter, completing the picture of wave-particle duality (radiation is particle-like; matter is wave-like).
questions.explanation: Setup, diffraction peak, wavelength match, conclusion.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A metal contains many free electrons that are held inside it by the attraction of the positive lattice ions. To remove an electron from the surface, a minimum energy called the work function must be supplied. This energy can be provided in different ways.

(i) Define the work function.
(ii) In what unit is it usually measured?
(iii) Name the four types of electron emission.
(iv) Which type occurs when the metal is heated?
questions.answer:
(i) The work function is the minimum energy required to just free an electron from the surface of a metal.
(ii) It is usually measured in electron-volt (eV), where 1 eV = 1.6 x 10^-19 J.
(iii) Thermionic emission, field emission, photoelectric emission and secondary emission.
(iv) Thermionic emission occurs when the metal is heated.
questions.explanation: Definition, unit, four types, thermionic on heating.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The work function of a metal is related to its threshold frequency by phi0 = h f0. For a certain metal the work function is 3.3 x 10^-19 J. (Take h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s, c = 3 x 10^8 m/s.)

(i) What is the threshold frequency of the metal?
(ii) What is the threshold wavelength?
(iii) Express the work function in eV.
(iv) Will red light of wavelength 700 nm eject electrons from this metal?
questions.answer:
(i) f0 = phi0/h = 3.3 x 10^-19 / 6.63 x 10^-34 = 4.98 x 10^14 Hz (about 5.0 x 10^14 Hz).
(ii) lambda0 = c/f0 = 3 x 10^8 / 4.98 x 10^14 = 6.02 x 10^-7 m = 602 nm.
(iii) phi0 = 3.3 x 10^-19 / 1.6 x 10^-19 = 2.06 eV.
(iv) Red light of 700 nm has a longer wavelength (lower frequency) than the threshold 602 nm, so its photon energy (1240/700 = 1.77 eV) is less than the work function (2.06 eV). Hence it will NOT eject electrons.
questions.explanation: f0=phi0/h; lambda0=c/f0; phi0 in eV; 700 nm below threshold.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In a photoelectric experiment, monochromatic light falls on an emitter and the photoelectric current is measured for different values of intensity, collector potential and frequency.

(i) How does the photoelectric current depend on the intensity of light?
(ii) What is the saturation current?
(iii) Define the stopping potential.
(iv) What happens to the current if the frequency of light is below the threshold frequency?
questions.answer:
(i) The photoelectric current is directly proportional to the intensity of the incident light (for fixed frequency and potential).
(ii) The saturation current is the maximum, constant photoelectric current reached when the collector potential is large enough for every emitted photoelectron to be collected.
(iii) The stopping potential is the retarding voltage at which the photoelectric current just becomes zero; e V0 = K_max.
(iv) If the frequency is below the threshold frequency, no photoelectrons are emitted and the current is zero, whatever the intensity.
questions.explanation: Current vs intensity; saturation; stopping potential; below f0 no current.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The classical wave theory of light successfully explains interference and diffraction but fails to explain the photoelectric effect. According to that theory, the energy of a light wave depends on its intensity and is spread over the wavefront.

(i) What does the wave theory predict about the existence of a threshold frequency?
(ii) What does it predict about the effect of intensity on the maximum kinetic energy?
(iii) What does it predict about a time lag for feeble light?
(iv) Which of these predictions agree with experiment?
questions.answer:
(i) The wave theory predicts NO threshold frequency - light of any frequency, if intense enough, should eject electrons.
(ii) It predicts that the maximum kinetic energy should increase with intensity (brighter light).
(iii) It predicts a measurable time lag for feeble light, since an electron must slowly accumulate energy.
(iv) None of these agree with experiment: there IS a threshold frequency, K_max is independent of intensity (it depends on frequency), and emission is instantaneous. Hence the wave theory fails.
questions.explanation: Wave-theory predictions all contradicted by experiment.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Einstein's photoelectric equation is K_max = h f - phi0. Light of wavelength 400 nm falls on a metal whose work function is 2.0 eV. (Use photon energy in eV = 1240/wavelength in nm.)

(i) Find the energy of each photon.
(ii) Find the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons.
(iii) Find the stopping potential.
(iv) What would happen if light of wavelength 700 nm were used instead?
questions.answer:
(i) E = 1240/400 = 3.1 eV.
(ii) K_max = E - phi0 = 3.1 - 2.0 = 1.1 eV.
(iii) e V0 = K_max, so V0 = 1.1 V.
(iv) For 700 nm, E = 1240/700 = 1.77 eV, which is less than the work function 2.0 eV. So no photoelectrons would be emitted.
questions.explanation: E, K_max, V0, and 700 nm below threshold.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In an experiment, the stopping potential V0 is measured for different frequencies f of the incident light, and a graph of V0 against f is plotted. It is found to be a straight line.

(i) Write the equation relating V0 and f.
(ii) What does the slope of the line represent?
(iii) How can Planck's constant be found from the graph?
(iv) What does the intercept on the frequency axis represent?
questions.answer:
(i) e V0 = h f - phi0, i.e. V0 = (h/e) f - phi0/e.
(ii) The slope of the V0 versus f line represents h/e.
(iii) Multiply the measured slope (h/e) by the electronic charge e to obtain Planck's constant h. (This is how Millikan measured h in 1916.)
(iv) The intercept on the frequency axis (where V0 = 0) represents the threshold frequency f0 = phi0/h of the metal.
questions.explanation: V0=(h/e)f-phi0/e; slope h/e; h = slope x e; intercept = f0.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A photon is a quantum of electromagnetic radiation. It has energy E = h f = h c/lambda and momentum p = h/lambda. Consider light of wavelength 500 nm. (Take h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s, c = 3 x 10^8 m/s.)

(i) Calculate the energy of one photon in joule.
(ii) Express this energy in eV.
(iii) Calculate the momentum of the photon.
(iv) State two properties of a photon.
questions.answer:
(i) E = h c/lambda = (6.63 x 10^-34 x 3 x 10^8)/(500 x 10^-9) = 3.98 x 10^-19 J.
(ii) E = 3.98 x 10^-19 / 1.6 x 10^-19 = 2.49 eV (about 2.48 eV from 1240/500).
(iii) p = h/lambda = 6.63 x 10^-34/(500 x 10^-9) = 1.33 x 10^-27 kg m/s.
(iv) A photon has zero rest mass and is electrically neutral; it travels at the speed of light and carries momentum h/lambda. (Any two.)
questions.explanation: E in J and eV, momentum, properties.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

de Broglie proposed that a moving particle has an associated wave of wavelength lambda = h/(m v). For an electron accelerated through a potential difference of V volt, this reduces to lambda = 12.27/sqrt(V) angstrom.

(i) State the de Broglie hypothesis.
(ii) Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through 100 V.
(iii) How does the wavelength change if V is increased to 400 V?
(iv) Why is the wave nature of a moving cricket ball not observed?
questions.answer:
(i) de Broglie hypothesis: every moving material particle of momentum p = m v has an associated wave of wavelength lambda = h/p = h/(m v).
(ii) lambda = 12.27/sqrt(100) = 12.27/10 = 1.227 angstrom.
(iii) For 400 V, lambda = 12.27/sqrt(400) = 12.27/20 = 0.61 angstrom, i.e. it is halved (since increasing V four times halves lambda).
(iv) A cricket ball has a very large mass, so its de Broglie wavelength lambda = h/(m v) is far too small (h is extremely small) to produce any observable diffraction. Hence its wave nature is not noticed.
questions.explanation: Hypothesis; 100 V and 400 V values; large-mass explanation.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In 1927 Davisson and Germer directed a beam of electrons, accelerated through a known potential, at a single crystal of nickel and measured the intensity of the scattered electrons at various angles.

(i) What was observed in the scattered electron intensity?
(ii) At what voltage and angle did a strong peak appear?
(iii) What wavelength did the de Broglie formula predict for these electrons?
(iv) What did the experiment establish?
questions.answer:
(i) The scattered intensity showed a distinct PEAK (maximum) at a particular scattering angle for a particular accelerating voltage - a diffraction maximum.
(ii) A strong peak appeared for electrons accelerated through 54 V, at a scattering angle of 50 degrees.
(iii) The de Broglie formula predicts lambda = 12.27/sqrt(54) = 1.67 angstrom, in close agreement with the value (about 1.65 angstrom) found from the crystal geometry.
(iv) The experiment established the WAVE NATURE OF MATTER - electrons are diffracted like waves, with the wavelength predicted by de Broglie.
questions.explanation: Peak observed; 54 V, 50 deg; 1.67 angstrom; wave nature confirmed.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The dual nature of radiation and matter means that radiation can behave like particles and matter can behave like waves. The photoelectric effect shows the particle nature of radiation, while the Davisson-Germer experiment shows the wave nature of matter.

(i) Which experiment shows the particle nature of radiation?
(ii) Which experiment shows the wave nature of matter?
(iii) Write the expression for the momentum of a photon and the de Broglie wavelength of a particle.
(iv) What common constant appears in both expressions?
questions.answer:
(i) The photoelectric effect shows the particle (photon) nature of radiation.
(ii) The Davisson-Germer electron-diffraction experiment shows the wave nature of matter.
(iii) Photon momentum p = h/lambda; de Broglie wavelength of a particle lambda = h/p = h/(m v).
(iv) Planck's constant h appears in both, linking the particle and wave descriptions and expressing the symmetry between radiation and matter.
questions.explanation: Photoelectric = particle radiation; Davisson-Germer = wave matter; both use h.
